info.description: The vessel calls of the week. Each call is two rows of the model's order book, <call>-D (discharge moves) and <call>-L (load moves): release is the berthing time, due is the planned departure, quantity is the number of container moves, and the free attribute `direction` is D or L. The containers leave by "out" stamped with entity.order_id, so the vessel turn time is the order's release-to-last-completion time in the order summary. The book lives in the model (Orders tab, CSV import), not in the asset, so one asset serves any schedule. Berth allocation is not modelled: the schedule says where and when each vessel berths. No input port.

info.description: A berth's ship-to-shore cranes as one pool. A container to discharge enters by "discharge_in", takes one crane for a cycle, is set down on the apron, a finite space of "Apron slots", and leaves by "discharge_out"; a container to load enters by "load_in", takes a crane for a cycle and leaves by "load_out". When the apron is full the crane stays blocked, holding the container, until a carrier takes one: 1 slot approximates coupled AGV operation, 3-4 slots decoupled straddle carriers. The pool (default "Quay cranes", capacity = cranes at the berth) is shared by both directions, so a crane works either one. The default cycle averages 1.7 minutes (about 35 gross moves per hour per crane); a constant 1.5 gives exactly 40.

info.description: The landside: trucks arrive at the rate of an hourly profile (trucks per hour), queue for a gate lane, are checked in, then drive to a yard block where its crane fetches a container from a bay drawn uniformly over the block's bays and sets it on the truck at the block's transfer point; the truck then leaves. The crane is the yard block's own fleet, named by "Yard crane" (<yard instance>/CT RTG), so trucks and carriers from the quay queue for the same crane. The truck turn time, from arrival at the gate to departure, is recorded per truck as the statistic "<instance>/truck turn time". Arrivals read the profile when each truck arrives, so a rate that jumps within one gap is seen late. No ports: trucks come and go here; the "gate" node marks the gate on the plan. The drive between gate and block is not modelled, every truck collects one container (no drop-offs or dual cycles yet), and a truck's container is never under another one (no reshuffles landside). The four Yard parameters must name one yard block and Bays used must not exceed that block's Bays; nothing checks that they agree.

info.description: One yard block served by one gantry crane (an RTG by default). A container enters by "in" and is given a bay drawn uniformly from the first "Bays" of the block; the crane travels from wherever it stands to that bay, picks the container, travels back to the block's transfer point (its "transfer" node, where the carriers and trucks are served) and sets it down, and the container leaves by "out". Each travel is the gantry's own hop: the longer of the gantry run along the block and the trolley run across it, plus the hoist time. With probability "Reshuffle share" the container is under another one and the crane hoists once more. The same cycle stands for stacking a container (transfer to bay) and retrieving one. The geometry lays out 30 bays 6.5 m apart (one TEU bay each) on the block's centre line, between the crane's runways, and the transfer point at the west end on the truck lane, 8 m across from the bays; the nodes are offsets from the block's centre, where its footprint is drawn. Move the bay nodes for another block. Set "Home node" to this block's transfer node, <instance>/transfer, so the crane starts there. The crane is the fleet <instance>/CT RTG, which a Truck gate names to share it. The crane's pick time reads the container's ct_reshuffle_s (seconds), which this block and the Truck gate set: any other TRANSPORT on this crane must set it too. Ceilings: no stack positions (a bay is a point, not rows and tiers); one crane per block, since two gantries on one runway do not see each other; a warm start does not carry where the crane stands.

info.description: The vehicles that carry containers between the quay and the yard: straddle carriers, AGVs, terminal tractors or reach stackers, picked from the Terminal vehicles catalogue. A container enters by "in" from the STATION it waits at; a vehicle drives to it on the path network, lifts it, drives it to the "Destination" STATION and sets it down, and the container goes on from that station. "done" is used only when Destination is empty and the container's routing has finished. Lift and set-down each take the class's lift time. Energy: a diesel or hybrid class draws its fuel kW while working and "Idle share" of it while waiting (1 l/h = 10 kW); an electric class (Fuel power 0) carries a battery of "Battery capacity" that its drive kW drains; below a quarter it drives to the nearest charger and works again at 90 %. "Charging strategy" adds topping up when idle (opportunity) or a pack swap at a swap station. Place Charger assets (Logistics library) for it, sized from the class's charger kW; their grid energy is the fleet's. A hybrid class counts as diesel: its battery is refilled by the engine, not a charger.

info.description: The meter: whatever the site cannot cover itself is imported and priced on a tariff profile, whatever it cannot use or store is exported up to the export limit, and the rest is curtailed. Import beyond the import limit is recorded as unserved demand rather than silently supplied. Emissions follow a grid intensity profile, so a sustainability assessment is the same run. Place exactly one per site: it is the slack that closes the energy balance. No ports: this is a continuous asset. A demand charge on the peak import power is billed once at the end of the run.

parameters.name: import_profile
parameters.label: Import tariff
parameters.help: Import price by hour of the day, EUR/kWh. A flat tariff is a one-value profile.

parameters.name: export_price
parameters.label: Export price
parameters.help: Paid for every exported kWh: it enters Total Cost as a negative cost.

parameters.name: intensity_profile
parameters.label: Grid carbon intensity
parameters.help: kg CO2e per imported kWh, by hour of the day. It drives Total Impact, which is deliberately generic: use it for water, waste or any other per-unit impact instead.

parameters.name: import_limit_kw
parameters.label: Import limit
parameters.help: Connection capacity. Demand beyond it is recorded as unserved energy, not supplied.

parameters.name: export_limit_kw
parameters.label: Export limit
parameters.help: Largest power the meter may export. Surplus beyond it is curtailed, which the curtailment flow accounts for.

parameters.name: demand_charge_per_kw
parameters.label: Demand charge
parameters.help: Billed once on the highest import power the site actually HELD (the import flow's Peak Rate), the way a network operator bills capacity. 0 for an energy-only tariff.

info.description: Puts the kW a resource, fleet or charger draws on the site bus, so the grid connection prices it. Name the equipment in Source: its busy, idle and other states come from the power it declares, and the draw follows those states through the run. Set Source before running; a name the model does not declare is reported as an unknown resource, fleet or charger. No ports: this is a continuous asset.

info.title: Container terminal: electrification
info.description: The quay-to-yard terminal with its straddle carriers' energy priced and counted: diesel as it is, battery straddle carriers charging opportunistically, and AGVs on pack swap. The question it answers: what do energy cost, CO2 and the grid's peak become, and does the extra capital pay back? Read the flow summary (fuel and grid kWh, peak kW), the cost summary, and the investment case across scenarios. Illustrative figures.
